title: Open Joints
passage:
Above a window head, a vertical joint is deliberately left free of mortar every half-metre or so. Those gaps are the whole of the wall's drainage. In a long south-westerly the outer skin of brick wets through, as the specification assumes it will. The water that gets past it runs down into the cavity, onto a tray bedded in over the opening, which discharges it through the open joints. While the wind is still on the wall it pushes in at those same joints, and the tray holds what it has collected. The lull is when it lets go. Not all of the joints run, and none for long. A head that gives back nothing an hour after the wind drops is worth recording, though whether the tray has been obstructed by mortar dropped during the build, or is spilling into the cavity past a missing stop end, an open joint cannot say.
– Rhoswen Pellowden, building surveyor

questions.prompt: What is said about the open joints before the wind drops?

options.text: Every joint above the opening is running, which is exactly what those gaps are there for.
The brick is still soaking up the rain, so nothing has reached the tray yet.
Nothing comes out of them, which usually means the tray was laid without stop ends.
Whatever the tray has caught stays on it, because the wind presses in at those joints.

questions.rationale: TYPE-001 direct detail, key_derivation paraphrase_one_sentence. The passage states the answer once, in the sentence that gives the item its whole point: 'While the wind is still on the wall it pushes in at those same joints, and the tray holds what it has collected.' D recasts that in different words - the water already on the tray stays there, and the wind pressing inward at the joints is why - and adds nothing the text does not say. The two sentences on either side make the reading unambiguous: the water is on the tray during the storm (it 'runs down into the cavity, onto a tray bedded in over the opening'), and the discharge belongs to a different moment ('The lull is when it lets go'). A = quantifier upgrade plus the intuitive reading of a drain: it takes the passage's own account of what the gaps are for ('Those gaps are the whole of the wall's drainage') and asserts that they are therefore all discharging while it rains. Two things in the text defeat it. The tray 'holds what it has collected' while the wind is on the wall, so nothing is running yet; and even in the lull the passage limits the claim - 'Not all of the joints run, and none for long' - so 'every joint' is an absolutisation the text explicitly refuses. This is the option a reader who has not noticed the timing sentence will take. B = reversed sequence: it puts the wetting of the brickwork and the arrival of water on the tray in the wrong order, holding that the outer skin is still absorbing and that the tray is therefore still dry. It is tempting because it borrows the passage's own soaking ('the outer skin of brick wets through') and because a lag between rain and leak is what most readers assume. The text has already moved past it: the water 'that gets past it' is on the tray, which is why the tray has something to hold. C = half-right conjunction, and the strongest distractor. Its first clause is exactly right - nothing does come out of the joints while the wind blows - so a solver who checks only that far will stop. The second clause supplies the wrong cause and an unsupported frequency: the passage attributes the stoppage to the wind, not to a defect, and where it does discuss defects it says a dry head cannot be diagnosed from outside at all - 'whether the tray has been obstructed by mortar dropped during the build, or is spilling into the cavity past a missing stop end, an open joint cannot say'. C also transplants the diagnosis to the wrong moment: the note is taken an hour after the wind drops, not while it is blowing. Hedge balance: the key is a flat causal assertion with no hedge; the only hedged option ('usually', C) is wrong and the only absolutiser ('Every', A) is wrong, so neither 'pick the qualified answer' nor 'strip the absolutes' locates the key. Lengths under mech tokenisation: A 16, B 15, C 15, D 16 - the key is tied for longest rather than uniquely longest, and the option-length ratio is 1.07 against the 2.36 ELF cap.

generator_meta.mechanism_verification_note: PHYSICS CHECK, run 2026-08-26 before drafting, because batch15's TYPE-001 short was refuted at V-FINAL for stating rail thermal behaviour backwards. Four independent sources were read (via the Exa web-search MCP; this session's WebSearch budget was exhausted before generation began). (1) Brick Development Association technical sheet TIS-C6 'Rain penetration of brickwork walls' (assets.ctfassets.net/.../TIS-C6-RAIN-PENETRATION-OF-BRICKWORK-WALLS.pdf): 'The outer leaf of masonry construction is not watertight'; water is expected 'to run freely down the inside of the outer leaf and be re-directed outwards via weep-holes'; and, in its exposure table, severe exposure gives 'Standing water in cavity tray (drains from weepholes when wind drops)'. That last cell is the exact directional claim the item turns on. (2) Brickability 'Resisting Rainwater Penetration': 'in conditions of persistent driving rain, water will penetrate the outer leaf and run down its inner surface within the cavity'; cavity trays over openings 'with stop ends and weepholes'; weepholes 'in vertical cross joints at intervals not greater than 450mm', 'not less than two weepholes over each opening'; stop ends 'prevent the possibility of water in the cavity running down onto the tray and being thrown off its ends into the cavity'; and, on the same page, rain penetration 'due to high winds blowing into cavity walls through weepholes and moving water up beyond the upstand of dpc trays'. (3) MPA Mortar Data Sheet 12: water enters 'generally through cracks at the interface between the masonry units and mortar' and 'will flow down the inside face of the outer leaf and be discharged out of the cavity usually through weepholes'; mortar droppings in the cavity deflect water to the inner leaf. (4) LABC, 'Installing site-formed cavity trays': trays 'directly above the opening/lintel', a stop end 'at each end', weepholes 'in the outer leaf immediately above the cavity tray', and 'Ensure the cavity trays are kept free of mortar droppings'. Every directional claim in the passage was checked against these: outer leaf porous by design (not a barrier) - confirmed; water crosses INWARD and runs DOWN the cavity face - confirmed; tray catches and turns it OUTWARD through the open perpends - confirmed; wind on the face pushes IN at those holes and holds the water on the tray, which drains when the wind drops - confirmed by (1) and (2); mortar droppings dam a tray and a missing stop end lets the tray spill into the cavity - confirmed by (2), (3), (4); spacing 'every half-metre or so' sits inside the cited 450 mm maximum without quoting a figure. Two claims are the writer's observation rather than a sourced standard and are framed as such in the passage: that not all of the joints run and none for long, and that a head giving nothing back an hour after the wind drops is worth a note. Both are consistent with (1)'s exposure table; neither is asserted as a rule of the trade.
